title: Esther Speaks and Haman Falls
summary: At the second banquet the king again asks Esther for her request, and she finally pleads for her own life and the lives of her people, who have been sold to destruction. When the king demands to know who is responsible, she names Haman. The king storms into the garden, returns to find Haman fallen on Esther's couch begging for his life, and on the word of the eunuch Harbonah orders Haman hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai.
story: Chapter 6 ended with Haman humiliated and hurried off to Esther's second banquet, his advisers already predicting his fall. The suspense Esther created in chapter 5 now breaks. This short chapter is the climax of the book's conflict between Haman and the Jews, and it resolves the personal threat with shocking speed. Yet it does not resolve everything. Haman is dead, but his decree still stands, sealed with the king's ring and unchangeable under Persian law, and the Jews throughout the empire are still marked for destruction on the thirteenth of Adar. Chapter 8 must deal with that.
historical:
The setting is still the palace at Susa under Xerxes (486 to 465 BC), in about his twelfth year. Palace gardens were a feature of Persian royal architecture; the Persian word that came into Greek as paradeisos, and eventually into English as paradise, referred to such enclosed royal parks. The king's sudden rage and quick sentence fit the picture of Persian kings in Greek sources as capable of swift and severe judgments at court.

Esther's accusation also exposes something the king may not have fully understood. Haman had asked permission to destroy an unnamed people whose laws were different (3:8), and had offered ten thousand talents of silver to the royal treasury. The king now learns that the people in question include his own queen. Whether he had grasped the scale of the plan before is not clear from the text, and the narrator shows him more interested in the insult to himself than in the fate of a people.
cultural:
At a Persian banquet guests reclined on couches, as Greeks and later Romans did. That detail explains the scene in verse 8: Haman, pleading for his life, falls onto the couch where Esther is reclining, just as the king returns. Court protocol in the ancient Near East strictly limited contact between men and the king's women, and even approaching the queen this closely could be read as a grave offense. The king's charge that Haman meant to assault the queen may be a deliberate misreading, but in that world it sealed his fate.

The covering of Haman's face (verse 8) is not explained. Many interpreters take it as a sign of condemnation, like a condemned man's face covered before execution; others think it reflects shame. Either way it marks the moment Haman is finished. Harbonah, one of the king's eunuchs, appears briefly as the one who mentions the gallows, showing how quickly court officials could turn against a fallen favorite.
literary: The chapter is tightly built around speech and reversal. Esther's plea (verses 3-4) is carefully framed: she speaks first of her own life and then of her people's, she uses the language of Haman's decree (destruction, death, and annihilation, echoing 3:13), and she adds that she would have kept silent if they had only been sold as slaves. Her naming of Haman is delayed to the end of her sentence for effect. The narrator then uses the image of falling: Haman's advisers said he would fall before Mordecai (6:13), and now he literally falls on the couch. The chapter closes with justice matching the crime exactly: Haman is hanged on the gallows he prepared for Mordecai, and only then does the king's fury subside.

outline.t: The king asks again at the second banquet
Esther pleads for her life and her people
The king's fury and Haman's fatal plea
Haman is hanged on his own gallows

doctrines.note: Haman's end fits the biblical pattern in which the wicked fall into the pit they dug for others (Psalm 7:15-16). The chapter shows justice working through a pagan king, bringing the evildoer's schemes back on his own head.

Esther's patience, the king's discovery in chapter 6, and Haman's desperate misstep all combine at this moment. No one in the story sees the whole picture, but every thread comes together to expose the enemy of the Jews.

Esther identifies herself with her people at the risk of her life, asking for her life and the lives of her people together. Her solidarity shows that belonging to God's people is not something a person can abandon for safety.

words.note: Makar, to sell. Esther says she and her people have been sold, picking up Haman's offer of silver to the treasury in chapter 3. Her word turns the financial language of the decree into what it really was: the purchase of a people's death.

Tsar, adversary or enemy, one who presses or distresses. Esther names Haman the adversary and enemy, and the pairing with oyev (enemy) gives her accusation weight. Haman is called the enemy of the Jews throughout the rest of the book.

Kavash, to subdue or bring into bondage, and in this context to assault or force. The king uses it of what he claims Haman intends against the queen. The same verb appears in Genesis 1:28 for subduing the earth; its range runs from rightful rule to violent domination.
Shakhakh, to subside or abate. It closes the chapter: only after Haman is hanged does the king's fury subside. The same verb is used when the flood waters subside in Genesis 8:1.

christ: The chapter shows evil undone by its own design: the gallows Haman built for an innocent man becomes his own place of death. The New Testament sees the cross as God's great reversal of evil, where the powers that crucified Jesus were themselves defeated; Paul writes that God “disarmed the powers and authorities” and “made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross” (Colossians 2:15). The connection is thematic: Haman is not a figure of Christ, and his death is judgment, not sacrifice. The contrast is also instructive. Esther pleads for her people's lives before a king who can be moved; Christ intercedes for his people before a God who already loves them, and his own death secures their life.

hard.q: Is Esther cruel to let Haman die when he begs her for his life?
hard.a: Some readers are troubled that Esther says nothing when Haman falls before her pleading, and that the story seems to delight in his downfall. It is worth remembering what Haman had done: he had arranged the killing of every Jew in the empire, including children, and had built a gallows for Mordecai that morning. His plea comes only once he is exposed, not from repentance. The decision to execute him belongs to the king, and nothing suggests Esther had power to override a furious Persian monarch, or that sparing Haman would have removed the decree that still threatened her people. Others note that the book's world is not the world of the Sermon on the Mount, and that the narrator reports without comment. The Bible elsewhere calls believers to love enemies and to leave vengeance to God, and it also affirms that governing authorities may justly punish grave wrongdoing. Esther's silence is best read as the end of a deadly conflict rather than as a model of personal response to enemies.

questions: Esther speaks first of her own life and then of her people's. What does it mean to stand openly with others who are under threat?
Haman falls into the trap he set for someone else. Where have you seen harm return upon the one who planned it?
Justice in this chapter comes swiftly, but the danger to the Jews remains. How do you live between a partial victory and a threat that hasn't yet passed?
